profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a national health policy innovation lab evaluating a draft adaptation of the Advance Value Framework for use beyond pharmaceutical HTA, specifically for comparing digital therapeutics, gene therapies, and hospital-at-home programs within a cross-sector pilot. The team already has a proposed value tree, draft scoring sheets, and a reviewer guide; this meeting is to judge whether the design is ready for pilot testing with an external advisory panel. The agenda is to review whether the current framework preserves the logic of the original Advance Value Framework while remaining usable across intervention types, check whether the scoring workflow is 'complete,' and decide what revisions are needed before circulating the pilot pack. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on sending the framework for pilot review, plus a short list of edits.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: MCDA design, health economics, preference elicitation, evidence synthesis
members.background: A former HTA methods advisor who now leads framework design for cross-sector evaluation tools; she has adapted pharmaceutical assessment methods for public-sector procurement and policy pilots.
members.private_state: She wants the framework approved for pilot circulation this week because the external advisory panel has already been booked, and she is mainly worried about preserving methodological coherence with MAVT principles while making only light edits.
hidden_assumptions: If the framework is described as 'generic,' reviewers will understand that some bottom-level attributes can be interpreted differently across intervention classes without rewriting the core tree.
A 'complete' pilot pack means the value tree, scoring scales, and worked examples are internally consistent enough for structured feedback, even if some evidence guidance is still provisional.
The 'reference case' for scoring is the standard care comparator already specified in the pilot brief, so it does not need to be restated in each criterion note.
When the team says 'innovation,' they naturally mean non-duplicative therapeutic and service contribution beyond current pathway options, not novelty in a purely technical sense.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Policy operations, payer decision processes, review workflow design, stakeholder usability testing
members.background: He previously managed appraisal operations for a regional payer consortium and now focuses on whether analytical tools can be applied consistently by mixed reviewer panels with limited training.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid sending out a framework that looks polished but produces inconsistent panel scoring, and he is especially concerned about practical interpretability for non-method experts on the advisory panel.
hidden_assumptions: If a framework is 'generic,' every bottom-level attribute and anchor description should work literally the same way across intervention classes, otherwise reviewers will improvise.
A 'complete' design review package means a panel could use it tomorrow with minimal facilitation and arrive at reproducible scoring decisions.
The 'reference case' for scoring each option is the currently funded option in that delivery setting, which may differ across hospitals and payers unless explicitly fixed.
When people say 'innovation,' they usually include implementation novelty, data infrastructure novelty, and procurement novelty if those features change adoption conditions.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'generic' value tree
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the framework should stay 'generic' across intervention types
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the top and mid-level structure should remain stable, while some bottom-level attribute interpretations and examples can vary by intervention class.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the framework should be directly and uniformly interpretable at the attribute level with no class-specific reinterpretation needed by reviewers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In MCDA and policy design settings, 'generic' is a positively loaded term that sounds like obvious agreement; both assume their interpretation is standard and neither expects the other to mean something narrower or stricter.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the design is 'complete' for pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the pack is 'complete' and 'ready for pilot review'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 judges completeness by methodological sufficiency for informed expert critique: stable value tree, draft scoring functions, and enough documentation to collect structured feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 judges completeness by operational readiness for near-live use: unambiguous instructions, explicit evidence handling rules, and enough standardization for consistent scoring by a mixed panel.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design reviews often use 'ready,' 'complete,' and 'good enough for pilot' as routine shorthand; because both support piloting in principle, the deeper difference in acceptance threshold remains hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: Which comparator is implied by the 'reference case'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to scoring against 'the reference case' or 'current practice'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot brief's designated standard-of-care comparator applies globally across all candidate interventions and criteria.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes reviewers will anchor judgments to whatever treatment or service configuration is currently funded in their own institutional context unless the guide restates a single comparator repeatedly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to comparator-based appraisal and believe the context is already shared; because no one is proposing a different comparator explicitly, the missing common presupposition stays invisible.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse keeping 'innovation' in the framework
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats innovation as bounded to therapeutic or care-pathway contribution already linked to patient and system value, excluding implementation mechanics unless they affect other criteria.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats innovation as also including implementation architecture, data interoperability, contracting novelty, and deployment model because these shape real-world distinctiveness for payers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both favor retaining the criterion and speak approvingly about capturing 'innovation,' so the disagreement hides in the boundary of what is folded under that label rather than in whether the criterion exists.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to get out this week so the advisory panel slot isn't wasted. The core question is whether the framework still respects MAVT logic while being generic in the sense that the top and middle structure hold across intervention classes, even if some lower-level attributes need to be read through class-specific examples. For pilot purposes, the pack is complete if the tree, scales, and examples are coherent enough to elicit disciplined feedback.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I thought we could keep this focused on two questions: first, whether the adapted Advance-based framework stays generic enough for a cross-sector pilot, and second, whether the pack is complete and ready for pilot review this week. My view is that the core structure is now in a good place, so I'd like us to pressure-test the remaining edits rather than reopen the architecture.

turns.inner_thought: The structure is promising, but I don't want us sending something that looks finished and then falls apart in a mixed panel. For me, complete means people could pick it up tomorrow with minimal hand-holding and score in a reasonably reproducible way. If they have to infer too much, the pilot will tell us more about facilitation than about the framework.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the overall structure is strong. The main thing I want to test is whether a mixed reviewer panel could use the pack consistently in a pilot without much facilitation. If we're saying it's complete and ready for pilot review, I'd want that to be true from the panel's point of view as well as ours.

turns.inner_thought: I should emphasize stability of the domains and keep the conversation away from rewriting bottom-level content. A generic framework doesn't require identical phrasing to do all the work across digital therapeutics, gene therapies, and hospital-at-home; it just needs a common value logic with examples that help reviewers map the specifics.
turns.utterance: Right. If I walk through the tree briefly, I think the strength is that the top-level domains and the mid-level logic remain stable across the three intervention types. That gives us a generic framework in the way we'd want for the pilot. Under a few attributes, the examples may look a little different for digital therapeutics, gene therapies, and hospital-at-home, but the overall structure is doing the same job.

turns.inner_thought: I like the stable architecture, but the lower-level wording still matters. If it's truly generic, reviewers shouldn't have to mentally remap an attribute depending on class. That's exactly where inconsistency creeps in with mixed panels. I need to nudge toward uniform interpretation without sounding like I'm challenging the whole tree.
turns.utterance: Yes, I like the generic design. My only caution is that each attribute should read the same way to reviewers across all three intervention classes, otherwise panelists may end up reinterpreting terms on the fly. If we can tighten the wording at that level, I think the structure will travel well.

turns.inner_thought: The scoring materials are already anchored to the standard-care comparator in the pilot brief, so I don't want to clutter every criterion note by restating it. Also, innovation belongs in the tree as therapeutic or care-pathway contribution beyond current options; if we let it sprawl, we'll duplicate other criteria. For pilot review, this is complete enough to test burden, therapeutic impact, safety, innovation, and socioeconomic impact coherently.
turns.utterance: On the scoring sheets, I think we're already in reasonable shape because they're anchored against the reference case. That should be enough for the pilot to react to the main domains—burden, therapeutic impact, safety, innovation, and socioeconomic impact—without us trying to over-engineer every note before we've had external feedback.

turns.inner_thought: The domains are right, but 'current practice' is exactly where reviewers diverge if the guide doesn't keep them aligned; they'll default to what's funded in their own setting. And on innovation, I still think people will expect implementation and contracting novelty to count if those features affect adoption. I need to raise both as usability issues, not methodological objections.
turns.utterance: I agree the domains are the right ones. The place I still stumble a bit is whether the guide gives a clear enough reminder of what current practice means for reviewers when they're scoring against the reference case. And on innovation, do we want the examples to speak a little more to implementation or contracting differences as well, just so people know how to read that criterion?

turns.inner_thought: The pilot brief already fixes the comparator, so I don't think we should act as if that's open. On innovation, I need to keep it bounded; implementation mechanics can be reflected elsewhere if relevant, but I don't want criterion overlap. Best to reassure him without inviting a redesign.
turns.utterance: My instinct is that the pilot brief already fixes the reference case, so I wouldn't want to overload the criterion notes with repeated reminders unless we think readers are genuinely missing it. On innovation, I'm happy to keep it in the framework, but I'd want it focused enough that it doesn't start collapsing into socioeconomic impact or the delivery-feasibility material.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that for now, but my bar for complete is still practical use. If the external panel can't score with what's in front of them, we'll get noise. I should state the operational expectation plainly without forcing a debate over definitions.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I suppose the way I'd phrase it is that, for the pack to feel complete, panelists should be able to score tomorrow using only the guide, the worked examples, and the criterion notes. If we think that's basically true after a light pass, then I'd be comfortable calling it ready for pilot review.

turns.inner_thought: He's still using a near-live readiness standard. I need to re-anchor this as a design review pilot, not a full operational launch. Completeness here is about stable MAVT logic, defensible scales, and a workable weights process so experts can critique constructively before we polish facilitation details.
turns.utterance: I agree with the direction of that, though I would frame the pilot a little differently. For a design review pilot, complete mainly means the MAVT logic is holding, the weights workflow is stable, and the attribute scales are settled enough that external experts can challenge them constructively before we do any final operational fine-tuning.

turns.inner_thought: We're probably not going to resolve the threshold today, so better to propose edits that reduce risk. I still want more uniform attribute wording and one explicit prompt on how to think about current practice, because otherwise reviewers will anchor locally. Small changes, big gain in consistency.
turns.utterance: That's fair. In that case, my suggestion would be a light edit pass rather than anything structural: tighten some wording so the generic attributes land more uniformly, and add one more note on how reviewers should think about the reference case in practice. I think that would take a lot of friction out of the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Good—minor edits only. I can accept wording refinements and a brief note, as long as the tree stays intact and we don't broaden innovation into a catch-all. That gets us to circulation this week and preserves methodological coherence.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with that. I'll do a minor wording pass, keep innovation in the tree, and add a brief boundary note there so the criterion reads cleanly without changing the structure. If we preserve the current architecture, I think we can circulate the pack after those edits.

turns.inner_thought: With those edits, this is good enough to put in front of the panel. I still expect some facilitation issues, but at least the pack will be closer to something people can use consistently. For my purposes, that gets it to complete enough and usable enough to proceed.
turns.utterance: Great. On that basis, I'm supportive of pilot circulation after the edits. The structure is strong, and with those clarifications I think the framework will feel complete and usable for the external panel.
